lessons.title: What Is Animal Nutrition and Why Does It Matter? — Launching the Anchoring Phenomenon

quiz.prompt: On a maize farm in Kakamega, a learner sees insects damaging maize plants. One insect leaves ragged holes in the leaves. Which insect is it?
choices: Grasshopper
Mosquito
Aphid
Fish eagle
quiz.rationale: The farm scene describes grasshoppers chewing ragged holes through maize leaves. Aphids cluster on stems and leave the leaves intact. Mosquitoes feed on blood, and the fish eagle is a bird at Lake Nakuru.
quiz.placement: Phase 1 (Predict): reading the Kakamega farm scenario and Lake Nakuru scene

quiz.prompt: During the prediction activity, a classmate writes: 'Mosquitoes can drink blood because they are stronger than grasshoppers.' You have only just started the lesson. What is the best way to treat this prediction?
choices: Record it under 'Our Starting Ideas' and check it later against evidence
Mark it wrong straight away and cross it out
Ignore it because it is not a real idea
Accept it as the final answer so the class can stop investigating
quiz.rationale: In this lesson, predictions are not corrected at the start. They are written on the board as starting ideas and revisited once evidence has been gathered.
quiz.placement: Phase 1 (Predict): recording predictions on the board under 'Our Starting Ideas'

quiz.prompt: A learner watches a mosquito feeding on skin and writes an observation in a chart. Which observation is the most specific and best based on evidence?
choices: The mosquito bit the skin
The mosquito pushed a thin tube into the skin
The mosquito was hungry
The mosquito is stronger than other insects
quiz.rationale: A good observation describes exactly what can be seen, including the shape of the part touching the food. 'A thin tube pushed into the skin' does this. 'Bit' is vague, and 'stronger' and 'hungry' are ideas, not observations.
quiz.placement: Phase 2 (Observe): two-column observation chart during the video clips

quiz.prompt: At Lake Nakuru, thousands of flamingos sweep their bent beaks sideways through the water. Which action word from the class observation list best describes how a flamingo feeds?
choices: Chew
Filter
Pierce
Tear
quiz.rationale: The observation words listed were PIERCE, CHEW, SUCK SAP, FILTER and TEAR. A flamingo sweeping its beak through water is FILTER. Tearing belongs to the fish eagle, chewing to the grasshopper and piercing to the mosquito.
quiz.placement: Phase 2 (Observe): Clip 2, flamingo sweeping motion, and the board words PIERCE / CHEW / SUCK SAP / FILTER / TEAR

quiz.prompt: Which animal is matched correctly to how it was seen feeding?
choices: Grasshopper: pierces skin to take blood
Mosquito: filters tiny food from lake water
Aphid: sucks sap from a plant stem
Fish eagle: chews maize leaves
quiz.rationale: Aphids cluster on stems and take plant sap. The mosquito pierces skin for blood, the grasshopper chews leaves, and the fish eagle tears fish. The other pairings mix these up.
quiz.placement: Phase 2 (Observe): observation chart for all five animals (mosquito, grasshopper, aphid, flamingo, fish eagle)

quiz.prompt: In this lesson, animal nutrition is introduced as a new topic. Which statement best describes animal nutrition?
choices: The process by which animals take in oxygen from the air
The process by which animals get rid of waste from their bodies
The process by which animals obtain and use food for energy, growth and repair
The process by which green plants make food using sunlight
quiz.rationale: Animal nutrition is how animals obtain and use food for energy, growth and repair. Making food from sunlight is plant photosynthesis, taking in oxygen is breathing, and removing waste is excretion.
quiz.placement: Phase 3 (Explain): exit check question 'What do we call the process by which animals obtain and use food?'

quiz.prompt: At the end of the lesson, learners have studied the outside feeding structures of five animals. One learner asks: 'What happens inside the animal's body after the food gets in?' What is the status of this question?
choices: It has been fully answered by the feeding videos
It has been fully answered by the Structure → Function → Food table
It has been answered because the mosquito is stronger than the grasshopper
It is still an open question that the rest of the sub-strand will investigate
quiz.rationale: The lesson only looked at the outside feeding structures. What happens inside the animal is the 'Bridge to the Sub-Strand' and stays on the Driving Question Board to be investigated in later lessons.
quiz.placement: Phase 4 (DQB): Driving Question Board, questions about 'INSIDES' and the Bridge to the Sub-Strand

quiz.prompt: Learners are asked to draw a first annotated sketch model of one animal's feeding structure. Which statement best describes this 'starting model'?
choices: It is a final answer that will not be changed again
It should be copied from a textbook so that it has no mistakes
It shows the learner's current best thinking and will be revised in later lessons
It must be completely correct before it can be handed in
quiz.rationale: Learners are told the model is a STARTING model that does not need to be correct or complete. It is dated and revised in later lessons as understanding grows.
quiz.placement: Phase 5 (Model): first annotated sketch model of one animal's feeding structure

lessons.title: Chewing and Biting Mouthparts: How Mandibles Enable Mechanical Breakdown of Solid Food

quiz.prompt: A farmer in Kakamega finds maize leaves with ragged, irregular holes and torn edges. What physical property must the feeding tool of the insect that caused this damage have?
choices: It must be a long hollow tube that pierces the leaf surface
It must be soft and thin so it can suck sap from the leaf
It must be hard and toothed so it can cut and grind solid leaf tissue
It must be a smooth flap that only holds the leaf in place
quiz.rationale: Ragged, torn edges show that solid tissue was cut and ground by a hard, toothed tool. A soft or hollow tube would leave the leaf intact, not torn.
quiz.placement: Predict: describing the ragged maize leaf damage (image A) and the PREDICTED TOOL FEATURES column

quiz.prompt: A grasshopper has five main mouthpart components. Which structure is the most important chewing tool, being hardened and toothed and moving sideways to cut, crush and grind plant tissue?
choices: Labrum
Hypopharynx
Mandibles
Labium
quiz.rationale: The mandibles are hard, toothed and move sideways to cut and grind food. The labrum only holds food in place, even though it is at the front.
quiz.placement: Observe: close-read annotation of the Grasshopper Mouthpart Diagram handout

quiz.prompt: A learner says, "The labrum is at the front of the grasshopper's mouth, so it must do the cutting." Which reply is correct?
choices: Wrong. The labrum is a flap-like upper lip that holds food in place, while the mandibles do the cutting
Correct. The structure at the front always does the cutting
Wrong. The labrum is the part that mixes saliva with food
Correct. The labrum is hard and toothed like the mandibles
quiz.rationale: Position does not show function. The labrum is a soft flap that holds food, and the hardened toothed mandibles cut and grind. The hypopharynx is the part that helps mix saliva with food.
quiz.placement: Observe: probing the misconception that the labrum is the main cutting structure

quiz.prompt: Which pair of structures correctly matches a grasshopper mouthpart with its function?
choices: Hypopharynx: cuts food sideways; labrum: moves food towards the mandibles
Labium: forms a lower lip that stops food falling out; maxillae: move food towards the mandibles
Maxillae: grind food; labium: mixes saliva with food
Labium: cuts leaf tissue; maxillae: hold food in place as an upper lip
quiz.rationale: The labium is the lower lip that prevents food falling out, and the maxillae handle food and move it towards the mandibles. The other options mix up the functions.
quiz.placement: Observe: structured text read aloud about the five mouthpart components

quiz.prompt: Both grasshoppers and termites are crop pests in Kenya. Which statement best explains why both can damage plants in similar ways?
choices: Both have a hollow tube for sucking sap from stems
Both swallow plant material whole without any mouthparts
Both have hard, toothed chewing mouthparts that can cut and grind solid plant material
Both have soft mouthparts that dissolve plant tissue before eating it
quiz.rationale: Grasshoppers and termites both have chewing mouthparts with hard, toothed mandibles adapted to solid plant material. This shows a structural pattern across species.
quiz.placement: Observe: termite mouthpart comparison with the grasshopper

quiz.prompt: Grasshoppers break maize leaves into small pieces using their mandibles, without changing the leaf chemically. What is this type of breakdown called?
choices: Chemical digestion
Egestion
Mechanical digestion
Absorption
quiz.rationale: Physical tearing, cutting and grinding by mouthparts is mechanical digestion. Chemical digestion needs enzymes to change the food chemically.
quiz.placement: Explain: sentence-stem explanation ("This type of breakdown is called...")

quiz.prompt: A farmer in Kakamega notices that termites are destroying the wooden posts of a fence. Using what you know about chewing mouthparts, how are the termites able to do this?
choices: They use hard, toothed mandibles to scrape and cut tiny pieces of wood, which is solid plant material
They use the soft labrum to tear the wood apart
They dissolve the wood with saliva before touching it
They pierce the wood with a hollow needle and suck out liquid
quiz.rationale: Termites have chewing mouthparts, and hard toothed mandibles can cut off tiny pieces of wood, which is solid plant material. The soft labrum only holds food.
quiz.placement: Explain: consolidation question about termites and fence posts

quiz.prompt: Could an insect with mandibles like a grasshopper's (hard, toothed blades for cutting and grinding) drink blood from your skin as a mosquito does? Choose the best reason.
choices: No, because such mandibles are built to cut and grind solid food, not to carry liquid
No, because mandibles are only found in grasshoppers
Yes, because all insects use the same mouthparts for every kind of food
Yes, because toothed mandibles are the best tool for sucking liquids
quiz.rationale: Hard, toothed mandibles suit solid food. Drinking blood needs a different structure, which Lesson 3 will explore. Mosquitoes do have mandibles, but they are thin and needle-like.
quiz.placement: Explain: seeding question "could a mosquito feed with mandibles shaped like these?"

quiz.prompt: A learner writes in her notebook, "The grasshopper chews with its teeth, like we do." What is the best correction?
choices: Grasshoppers chew only with the labium
Grasshoppers have teeth in their stomachs only
Grasshoppers have no mouthparts that can cut anything
The toothed edge is part of the mandible, a jointed mouthpart, not a set of teeth like ours
quiz.rationale: The toothed edge belongs to the mandible, a jointed mouthpart. Grasshoppers do not have teeth like humans.
quiz.placement: Explain: oral feedback on the statement "the grasshopper chews with its teeth"

quiz.prompt: In your cumulative model, you draw the mandibles with arrows showing sideways movement and an arrow to the ragged maize leaf. Which annotation best completes the entry?
choices: The leaf is dissolved by the mandibles into a liquid
Solid plant tissue is broken into smaller pieces by physical force before swallowing
The mandibles pump blood from the plant into the grasshopper
The mandibles break food down using enzymes into simple nutrients
quiz.rationale: Mandibles break solid plant tissue into smaller pieces by physical force (mechanical digestion), the first step in obtaining nutrients.
quiz.placement: Model: Cumulative Model inset showing mandibles and MECHANICAL DIGESTION

lessons.title: Piercing and Sucking Mouthparts: How Does a Mosquito Drink Blood but a Grasshopper Cannot?

quiz.prompt: A farmer in Kakamega sees maize plants wilting with aphids clustered on the stems, but the leaves have no holes or torn edges. What best explains why there is no visible chewing damage?
choices: Aphids eat the leaves only at night, and the plant repairs the holes by morning
Aphids chew the leaves so slowly that the holes are too small to see
Aphids push a needle-like stylet into the stem and suck phloem sap, so nothing is chewed or torn
Aphids inject a poison that dissolves the leaf surface and closes the holes
quiz.rationale: An aphid has piercing-sucking mouthparts. A fine stylet bundle slides into the stem and draws up liquid phloem sap, so the plant weakens and wilts without any chewing holes.
quiz.placement: Clip 1: aphids feeding on a plant stem (comparison observation chart, column 5: visible damage)

quiz.prompt: Which pair correctly matches each insect with the food it takes using its piercing-sucking mouthparts?
choices: Aphid: blood; female mosquito: phloem sap from a plant
Aphid: nectar from flowers only; female mosquito: solid leaf tissue
Aphid: phloem sap from a plant; female mosquito: blood
Aphid: solid leaf tissue; female mosquito: blood
quiz.rationale: Aphids pierce plant stems to reach liquid phloem sap. Female mosquitoes pierce skin to draw blood. Neither feeds on solid tissue.
quiz.placement: Clip 1 and Clip 2: aphid and mosquito rows of the comparison observation chart (column 2: food source)

quiz.prompt: In a straw model of a mosquito's mouthparts, two thin straws are taped side by side inside a wider straw. One thin straw is the food canal and the other is the salivary canal. Why does the real mouthpart need two separate channels?
choices: One channel carries blood up into the mosquito and the other carries saliva down into the skin
One channel is for the mosquito to breathe through and the other is for hearing
Both channels carry blood so that the mosquito can feed twice as fast
One channel is for the left side of the mouth and the other is for the right side
quiz.rationale: Food has to go in and saliva has to go out at the same time. The food canal carries blood upward and the salivary canal carries saliva into the tissue, so two channels are needed.
quiz.placement: Part A: physical modelling of the stylet (food canal vs salivary canal prompt)

quiz.prompt: A group builds a straw model of a piercing-sucking mouthpart. The wider outer straw (or foil tube) surrounds the inner stylet bundle. Which real part does it represent, and what is its job?
choices: The stylet blade, which cuts the skin open and tears it
The salivary canal, which carries blood to the gut
The food canal, which chews solid food into small pieces
The labium sheath, which protects and guides the stylet bundle as it enters the tissue
quiz.rationale: The labium forms the outer sheath. It protects and guides the inner stylet bundle, which slides forward into the skin or stem. It does not carry food or saliva.
quiz.placement: Part A: physical modelling of the stylet (labelling labium, food canal, salivary canal, stylet bundle)

quiz.prompt: After building the model, the teacher explains how the needle-like stylet bundle of a mosquito relates to the mouthparts of a grasshopper. Which statement is correct?
choices: The mosquito stylet is a single tube made from the grasshopper's labium alone
The mosquito stylet is made of the grasshopper's mandibles fused together into one thick tooth
The mosquito stylet is built from the same basic parts as a grasshopper's mouthparts, but each part is stretched into a thin blade
The mosquito stylet is a completely new structure that has nothing in common with a grasshopper's mouthparts
quiz.rationale: The stylet bundle uses the same parts as a chewing mouth (labrum, mandibles, maxillae, hypopharynx), but each is modified into a thin blade that pierces rather than chews.
quiz.placement: Part A: physical modelling, after groups finish (link to Lesson 2 mandibles question)

quiz.prompt: In the Kakamega evening, a learner is bitten by a mosquito. Which statement about mosquito feeding is correct?
choices: Only male mosquitoes take blood, and females feed on plant sap like aphids
Mosquitoes chew small pieces of skin with their mandibles and swallow them
Only female mosquitoes take blood, which they need for their eggs; males feed on nectar and plant juices
Both male and female mosquitoes take blood, because they need it to survive
quiz.rationale: Only female mosquitoes pierce skin and take blood, because they need it for their eggs. Males feed on nectar and plant juices, and no mosquito chews skin.
quiz.placement: Part A: physical modelling of the stylet (teacher note on female mosquitoes)

quiz.prompt: A tsetse fly has the same kind of piercing-sucking mouthparts as a mosquito. What does this tell you about its food, and why does it matter in Kenya?
choices: It feeds on nectar only, so it helps pollinate crops
It feeds on solid leaves, so it damages maize crops
It feeds on blood from cattle, wild animals and people, and can pass on trypanosomes that cause nagana and sleeping sickness
It feeds on phloem sap, so it spreads maize diseases
quiz.rationale: Piercing-sucking mouthparts take liquid food. The tsetse fly takes blood, so it can pass trypanosomes to cattle (nagana) and to people (sleeping sickness).
quiz.placement: Cumulative mouthpart diversity model: tsetse fly question (Kenyan context label: Western Kenya/Rift Valley)

quiz.prompt: A learner adds piercing-sucking mouthparts next to chewing mouthparts in the class mouthpart model. Which connecting statement is scientifically correct?
choices: Both types of mouthparts use the same blades to tear food, but only the chewing type swallows it
Chewing mouthparts use mandibles to break solid food, while piercing-sucking mouthparts use a needle-like stylet to reach liquid food without damaging the surface tissue
Chewing mouthparts reach liquid food, while piercing-sucking mouthparts use mandibles to break solid food
Piercing-sucking mouthparts are used for a different goal, because those insects do not need nutrients
quiz.rationale: All insects need nutrients, but the tools differ. Chewing mouthparts break up solid food, while piercing-sucking mouthparts use a stylet to take liquid sap or blood and leave the surface unchewed.
quiz.placement: Cumulative mouthpart diversity model: connecting statement and 'SAME GOAL, DIFFERENT TOOLS' arrow

lessons.title: Crushing and Tearing Bird Beaks: How Does a Fish Eagle Eat What a Hornbill Cannot?

quiz.prompt: An African fish eagle at Lake Naivasha has a beak that is sharply hooked, with a pointed tip and a strong base. Which feeding action is this beak best suited for?
choices: Piercing skin to suck blood
Chewing leaves into small pieces using side-to-side jaws
Gripping a slippery fish and tearing its flesh into pieces
Crushing hard fruits and seeds into a pulp
quiz.rationale: A hooked beak grips slippery prey and a sharp pointed tip tears flesh. Crushing is for blunt beaks, and piercing-sucking and chewing are insect mouthpart actions.
quiz.placement: Predict: photographs of the fish eagle and the African grey hornbill, predicting which bird eats flesh

quiz.prompt: An African grey hornbill in Arabuko-Sokoke Forest has a large beak with a casque, a curved but blunter tip, and a wide gape. Which food and feeding action fit these features best?
choices: Picking up and tossing fruits and insects into its wide mouth
Sucking plant sap through a thin tube
Gripping live tilapia with a sharp hooked tip
Tearing flesh from a carcass with sharp cutting edges
quiz.rationale: The blunter tip and wide gape suit picking up and tossing fruit and insects. The beak is not sharply hooked, so it is not suited to tearing flesh.
quiz.placement: Observe: resource sheet with four labelled beak diagrams and the observation table (hornbill row)

quiz.prompt: The fish eagle and the white-backed vulture both have hooked beaks. A learner says, "All hooked beaks are identical and do the same job." Which statement best shows why this is a misconception?
choices: The fish eagle's beak is hooked but the vulture's beak is straight and general-purpose
The vulture's beak is designed for crushing hard fruits, while the fish eagle's is designed for tearing
The two beaks differ only in colour, not in structure or function
The vulture has a sharp-edged hooked bill and a long bare neck for reaching into carcasses, while the fish eagle has a pointed tip and strong base for gripping live slippery fish
quiz.rationale: Both beaks are hooked, but the vulture's cutting edges and long bare neck suit feeding on carcasses, while the eagle's pointed tip and strong base suit gripping live fish. The pied crow, not the vulture, has the straight general-purpose beak.
quiz.placement: Observe: shared class table, discussion of fish eagle and vulture beak differences

quiz.prompt: Imagine a hornbill was given a fish eagle's beak. What would most likely happen when it tried to feed on fruit?
choices: It would feed easily, because every beak can handle any food
It would handle fruit easily, because a sharp hook is best for picking up fruit
It would grow a new beak shape within a few days to suit the fruit
It would struggle to pick up and toss fruit, because the eagle beak is adapted for gripping and tearing flesh, not for handling fruit
quiz.rationale: A beak is an adaptation matched to a particular food and feeding action. A hooked, tearing beak is a poor tool for picking up and tossing fruit, just as a grasshopper's mouthparts are wrong for drinking blood.
quiz.placement: Explain: beak-swap question (fish eagle given a hornbill beak and a hornbill given a fish eagle beak)

quiz.prompt: A learner writes: "The fish eagle changed its beak shape so that it could eat fish." Which response corrects this idea best?
choices: The learner is correct, because an animal's body changes to suit the food it eats
Beaks are inherited and shaped over many generations, so a chick hatches with the beak it will use as an adult
Beaks change shape each time a bird eats a different food
A bird chooses its beak shape when it is about to hatch from the egg
quiz.rationale: An adaptation is a structure shaped over many generations and inherited. An individual bird does not change its beak to suit what it eats.
quiz.placement: Explain: CER statements and the meaning of the word adaptation

quiz.prompt: A learner completes a table row for the fish eagle. Which pair of entries correctly separates the Food Accessed column from the Feeding Action column?
choices: Food accessed: hooked tip; Feeding action: tilapia
Food accessed: gripping and tearing; Feeding action: tilapia
Food accessed: crushing fruit; Feeding action: fish
Food accessed: tilapia (fish); Feeding action: gripping and tearing flesh
quiz.rationale: Food accessed is what the animal eats, here tilapia or fish. Feeding action is the physical thing the beak does to get it, here gripping and tearing.
quiz.placement: Model: extending the cumulative feeding-structures comparison table with CRUSHING AND TEARING BEAKS rows

quiz.prompt: Which statement correctly compares a fish eagle's beak with a mosquito's stylets?
choices: Both crush hard food between blunt surfaces
The eagle's hooked beak grips and tears solid flesh, while the mosquito's stylets pierce skin to suck liquid blood
Both pierce skin and suck liquid food
The eagle's beak sucks sap from plants, while the mosquito's stylets tear flesh
quiz.rationale: In both animals the structure fits the food. The eagle's hooked, pointed beak tears solid flesh, while the mosquito's thin stylets pierce skin to draw up liquid blood.
quiz.placement: Model: comparison sentence linking the fish eagle beak and the mosquito stylet

lessons.title: Probing and Filtering Bird Beaks: How Beak Morphology Reveals Diet and Habitat

quiz.prompt: A flamingo at Lake Nakuru has a bent beak with comb-like plates along its inner edges. Based on this beak, what does it most likely eat?
choices: Dead animals that it tears with a hooked beak
Large fish that it spears and tears apart
Nectar from tubular flowers
Microscopic algae and tiny animals strained from the water
quiz.rationale: A bent beak with comb-like plates (lamellae) is built for filtering. At Lake Nakuru flamingos feed mainly on microscopic algae, cyanobacteria and small animals in the water.
quiz.placement: Think-Pair-Share prediction: Lake Nakuru flamingo image and the 'OUR PREDICTIONS — Lesson 5' board

quiz.prompt: A flamingo feeds with its beak upside down in the water while its tongue pumps water through the beak. What is the main job of the comb-like lamellae along the beak edges?
choices: To suck up nectar from the water
To store water for the flamingo to drink later
To cut the food into small pieces
To trap tiny food particles while the water flows out
quiz.rationale: The lamellae work like a sieve. Water is pumped out through the gaps and the tiny food particles are left trapped inside the beak.
quiz.placement: Clip 1: flamingos filter-feeding at Lake Nakuru (freeze-frame on the beak interior)

quiz.prompt: A Variable Sunbird has a long, curved beak and a tubular tongue. What does it use this beak to do?
choices: Tear flesh from a dead animal
Reach into flowers to probe for nectar
Crush hard seeds and nuts
Filter algae from alkaline lake water
quiz.rationale: The long, curved beak fits into the flower tube and the tubular tongue draws up nectar. This is probing, not filtering, tearing or crushing.
quiz.placement: Clip 2: sunbird probing a flower for nectar, and the sunbird row of the Observation Chart

quiz.prompt: Why can a flamingo not feed on nectar from a narrow, tubular flower like the red-hot poker plant?
choices: Its beak is hooked for tearing flesh, which damages flowers
Nectar is poisonous to all water birds
Its beak is built to filter small particles from water, not to reach into a narrow flower tube
Flamingos are too heavy to stand near flowers
quiz.rationale: The flamingo's bent, lamellae-lined beak is a structural adaptation for filtering water. It does not have the long, curved shape and tubular tongue needed to reach nectar, so structure limits the diet.
quiz.placement: Part B: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning writing on why a flamingo cannot eat nectar

quiz.prompt: A learner writes a CER response about the flamingo. Which sentence is the REASONING part (the science that connects the evidence to the claim)?
choices: The flamingo's beak is adapted for filtering algae.
In the video, the flamingo holds its beak upside down in the water.
The comb-like plates work like a sieve: water passes out but food particles are trapped.
Flamingos gather in large groups at Lake Nakuru.
quiz.rationale: Reasoning explains how the structure does the job (the sieve mechanism). The first option is a claim, and the last two are observations (evidence), not a mechanism.
quiz.placement: Part B: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) writing and group sharing

quiz.prompt: A learner says, 'Flamingos at Lake Nakuru catch large fish by filtering them from the water.' Which response best corrects this idea?
choices: Wrong: the gaps between lamellae are tiny, so only very small food such as algae and small crustaceans is trapped.
Correct: the lamellae are sharp and cut fish into small pieces.
Correct: the tongue spears fish before they reach the lamellae.
Wrong: flamingos eat only flowers and nectar.
quiz.rationale: The lamellae form a fine sieve, so only microscopic algae, cyanobacteria and small animals small enough to be trapped are caught. Large fish are not filter-feeding food.
quiz.placement: Part A: annotated diagram of the flamingo beak and the teacher follow-up prompt on 'Could a fish pass between the lamellae?'

quiz.prompt: Learners have studied the grasshopper's mandibles, the aphid's and mosquito's stylets, the beaks of the fish eagle, vulture and hornbill, the flamingo's filter beak and the sunbird's probing beak. Which pattern sentence best describes ALL these feeding structures?
choices: Animals with larger mouthparts eat more food.
All feeding structures are used for sucking liquid food.
All animals use beaks to get their food.
Each feeding structure is shaped to suit the food the animal eats and how it gets it.
quiz.rationale: The model shows that structure matches function and diet across insects and birds. This is a generalisation, while the other options are wrong or apply to only some of the animals.
quiz.placement: Cumulative class model update: the 'pattern I see across ALL the feeding structures' sentence

lessons.title: Dentition in Mammals: Tooth Shape, Diet, and the Structure-Function Connection

quiz.prompt: A lion feeds mainly on the meat of animals such as wildebeest. Which type of tooth does a lion mainly use to stab and grip its prey?
choices: Canines
Molars
Dental pad
Incisors
quiz.rationale: Canines are long, pointed teeth that stab and grip prey. Incisors cut or nip, and molars crush or grind. A dental pad is not a tooth.
quiz.placement: Predict: Think-Pair-Share prediction of which tooth type each animal has the MOST of

quiz.prompt: A skull diagram shows the teeth on ONE side of a lion's mouth only. Upper jaw, one side: incisors 3, canines 1, premolars 3, molars 1. Lower jaw, one side: incisors 3, canines 1, premolars 2, molars 1. How many teeth does the lion have in its whole mouth?
quiz.rationale: One side has 8 upper teeth and 7 lower teeth, which is 15. The diagram shows one side only, so multiply by 2 to get 30 teeth.
quiz.placement: Observe: counting teeth on the labelled skull diagrams and evidence-gathering table

quiz.prompt: On one side of a cow's mouth, the upper jaw has incisors 0, canines 0, premolars 3 and molars 3. The lower jaw has incisors 3, canines 1, premolars 3 and molars 3. How many teeth does the cow have in its whole mouth?
quiz.rationale: Upper jaw, one side: 0+0+3+3 = 6. Lower jaw, one side: 3+1+3+3 = 10. One side has 16 teeth, so the whole mouth has 16 × 2 = 32.
quiz.placement: Explain: calculating the dental formula for the cow (Cow I 0/3, C 0/1, PM 3/3, M 3/3 × 2)

quiz.prompt: A lion has special teeth called carnassials. The last upper premolar and the first lower molar slide past each other like scissor blades. What is the main job of the carnassial teeth?
choices: Filtering small food particles from water
Holding grass against a dental pad
Shearing (slicing) meat
Grinding grass into a paste
quiz.rationale: Carnassial teeth work like scissor blades to shear flesh into pieces small enough to swallow. This links tooth shape to a meat diet.
quiz.placement: Explain: teacher modelling of the lion calculation and the carnassial teeth

quiz.prompt: A cow has no upper incisors or upper canines. Which statement best explains how this is an adaptation to its diet of grass?
choices: It uses a dental pad with its lower incisors to grip and pull grass, then grinds it with broad, ridged molars.
It swallows grass whole because its teeth are not needed for feeding.
It uses sharp canines to tear grass and does not need incisors.
It uses carnassial teeth to shear grass into small pieces.
quiz.rationale: The cow grips and pulls grass between the lower incisors and the upper dental pad. The broad, ridged molars then grind the tough plant material. Cows have no carnassials and no upper canines.
quiz.placement: Explain: Comparison Table and 3-sentence structure-function claim (cow: no upper incisors, dental pad)

quiz.prompt: A lion's canines pierce flesh, a mosquito's needle-like proboscis pierces skin, and a fish eagle's hooked beak tears fish. What pattern do these feeding structures show?
choices: Feeding structures are only for chewing, whatever the animal eats.
The shape of an animal's feeding structure fits the type of food it eats and how it obtains that food.
All animals of a similar size have the same feeding structures.
Animals that need food to survive all use the same tools to get it.
quiz.rationale: Different animals have very different feeding structures, and each is shaped for its own food and feeding action. This is the structure-function link the driving question explores.
quiz.placement: DQB: connecting mammal dentition to the mosquito proboscis and fish eagle beak evidence

quiz.prompt: A human has incisors, canines, premolars and molars (dental formula I 2/2, C 1/1, PM 2/2, M 3/3). The human diet includes both ugali and nyama choma. Which statement best links the human teeth to this diet?
choices: Humans have mostly flat, grinding teeth like a cow because meat is not eaten.
Humans have only incisors because food is cut before it is swallowed.
Humans have large, stabbing canines like a lion because meat is the main food.
Humans have a mixture of cutting, tearing and grinding teeth because they eat both plant and animal foods.
quiz.rationale: A human is an omnivore. The mixed set of teeth (incisors to cut, canines to tear, premolars and molars to grind) suits a diet of both plant and animal foods.
quiz.placement: Model: adding the 'Mammal Dentition' panel (lion, cow, human) to the cumulative Animal Feeding Structures model

lessons.title: The Human Digestive System: Tracing a Meal of Ugali and Sukuma Wiki

quiz.prompt: A group is laying out a life-sized model of the human digestive system. Which order shows the correct path of a swallowed meal of ugali and sukuma wiki?
choices: Mouth → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine → rectum
Mouth → oesophagus → stomach → large intestine → small intestine → rectum
Mouth → oesophagus → small intestine → stomach → large intestine → rectum
Mouth → stomach → oesophagus → small intestine → large intestine → rectum
quiz.rationale: Food moves from the mouth down the oesophagus into the stomach, then through the small intestine, the large intestine and finally the rectum. Putting the large intestine before the small intestine is a common sequencing error.
quiz.placement: Digestive System Kit: groups lay out the materials in sequence to form a life-sized model

quiz.prompt: The transport observer places the clay ball (a bolus of ugali) at the mouth station. What happens to the ugali here?
choices: Glucose from the ugali is absorbed into the blood
Pepsin and acid begin digesting the protein in the ugali
It is chewed into smaller pieces, and amylase in saliva starts changing starch into sugar
The ugali passes through unchanged until it reaches the stomach
quiz.rationale: Chewing is mechanical digestion, and salivary amylase begins chemical digestion of starch. Nothing is absorbed in the mouth, and pepsin and acid work in the stomach.
quiz.placement: Transport observer moves the clay ball through the model and narrates each stage

quiz.prompt: In the model, a string is run from the label LIVER with GALL BLADDER to the point where its juice enters the digestive tube. Where does the string end?
choices: At the large intestine
At the stomach
At the start of the small intestine
At the mouth
quiz.rationale: Bile from the liver and gall bladder, together with pancreatic juice, enters at the start of the small intestine. Saliva is the juice that enters at the mouth.
quiz.placement: Accessory organs: paper labels SALIVARY GLANDS, LIVER with GALL BLADDER and PANCREAS with strings to the tube

quiz.prompt: A learner says, "The stomach digests everything and absorbs the food into the blood." Which statement about the stomach is correct?
choices: It churns food, and acid and pepsin start digesting protein
It absorbs most glucose and amino acids into the blood
It absorbs water and passes out the fibre
It is a long tube lined with villi
quiz.rationale: The stomach is a muscular bag that churns food, and its acid and pepsin start protein digestion. Absorption of most nutrients happens in the small intestine, and water is absorbed in the large intestine.
quiz.placement: Meal Journey Table: the Stomach row

quiz.prompt: Sukuma wiki contains a lot of fibre. What happens to this fibre as it moves through the human digestive system?
choices: It is digested to glucose in the small intestine
It is not digested and leaves the body as faeces
It is absorbed into the blood in the stomach
It is broken down by pepsin and used for protein
quiz.rationale: Humans cannot digest fibre. It passes through the large intestine, where water is absorbed from it, and leaves as faeces.
quiz.placement: Meal Journey Table: what happens to sukuma wiki (fibre, vitamins, iron) at each organ

quiz.prompt: A mosquito drinks liquid blood, which is rich in protein. Compared with a human eating ugali, which statement is correct?
choices: The mosquito must chew the blood first, like a grasshopper, before it can be digested
The mosquito can skip chemical digestion because blood is already a liquid
The mosquito can skip chewing, but the blood proteins still have to be chemically digested and absorbed
The mosquito needs no digestion or absorption because blood is already part of a body
quiz.rationale: Liquid food does not need chewing or grinding (mechanical digestion). Blood proteins are still large molecules, so enzymes must break them down and the nutrients must be absorbed.
quiz.placement: Class discussion linking to the anchoring phenomenon: which stages can a mosquito skip?

quiz.prompt: The small intestine is about 6 to 7 metres long and its lining is covered in villi. Why does the small intestine have this structure?
choices: To absorb water and pass out the fibre
To churn the food and mix it with acid
To give a large surface area for absorbing glucose, amino acids, vitamins and iron into the blood
To store faeces until they leave the body
quiz.rationale: The length and villi greatly increase the surface area for absorbing digested nutrients. This is the same structure-function idea as the flamingo's lamellae, which increase surface area for filtering food.
quiz.placement: Revised Animal Nutrition Model panel: nutrients at the correct absorption site and the villi link to the flamingo's lamellae

lessons.title: Enzymes in Digestion: How Ugali and Sukuma Wiki Are Chemically Broken Down

quiz.prompt: A learner mixes a little unchewed, plain ugali with water and adds two drops of iodine solution. Ugali is rich in starch. What colour should the mixture turn?
choices: Colourless
Blue-black
Green
Brick-red
quiz.rationale: Iodine solution turns blue-black when starch is present, and unchewed ugali is mostly starch. Brick-red and green are Benedict's test colours for reducing sugar, not iodine colours.
quiz.placement: Predict: chewing plain ugali for two minutes and writing predictions about iodine and Benedict's tests

quiz.prompt: Chewed ugali and unchewed ugali are each mixed with water, heated with Benedict's reagent in a hot-water bath, and compared. The chewed sample turns green to orange, while the unchewed sample stays blue. What does this result show?
choices: Saliva made the ugali wet, which changes the colour of Benedict's reagent
Chewing turned the sugar in ugali into starch
Amylase in saliva broke some starch into reducing sugar during chewing
Unchewed ugali contains no starch at all
quiz.rationale: Benedict's reagent turns green, yellow or orange when reducing sugar is present. The sugar appeared only after chewing, so amylase in saliva must have changed starch into sugar. Wetness alone does not give a positive test.
quiz.placement: Observe: Benedict's test on tubes A (unchewed) and B (chewed) in the hot-water bath

quiz.prompt: A person has no pepsin in their stomach. They eat a meal of nyama choma (meat). Which food molecule will they have the most trouble digesting?
choices: Fat
Starch
Protein
Reducing sugar
quiz.rationale: Pepsin is the stomach enzyme that digests protein, and meat is rich in protein. Starch is digested by amylase and fat by lipase.
quiz.placement: Explain: guided question 1 on pepsin and nyama choma

quiz.prompt: Avocado contains fat. Which statement correctly describes how the fat is digested?
choices: Amylase in the mouth breaks fat into glucose
Lipase in the mouth breaks fat into amino acids
Pepsin in the stomach breaks fat into fatty acids and glycerol
Lipase in the small intestine breaks fat into fatty acids and glycerol
quiz.rationale: Lipase acts in the small intestine and splits fats into fatty acids and glycerol. Pepsin acts on proteins, amylase on starch, and fats do not form glucose or amino acids.
quiz.placement: Explain: two-column reference card and guided question 2 on lipase and avocado

quiz.prompt: After amylase has broken down one starch molecule in the mouth, what happens to the amylase?
choices: It is used up and must be replaced for each starch molecule
It turns into maltose
It joins the sugar and leaves with it
It is not used up and can break down many more starch molecules
quiz.rationale: Enzymes are biological catalysts, so they speed up reactions without being used up. One amylase molecule can digest many starch molecules.
quiz.placement: Explain: teacher addresses the misconception that enzymes are destroyed after one reaction

quiz.prompt: Which choice correctly matches each enzyme to where it acts in the human digestive system?
choices: Amylase: mouth and small intestine; pepsin: stomach; lipase: small intestine
Amylase: stomach; pepsin: mouth; lipase: small intestine
Amylase: mouth and small intestine; pepsin: small intestine; lipase: mouth
Amylase: small intestine only; pepsin: stomach; lipase: stomach
quiz.rationale: Amylase acts in the mouth and the small intestine, pepsin in the stomach, and lipase in the small intestine. The other choices place at least one enzyme in the wrong organ.
quiz.placement: Model: annotating the Lesson 7 digestive-system diagram with enzyme names and reaction sites

quiz.prompt: Why is chemical digestion by enzymes essential before nutrients can be absorbed into the body?
choices: It converts large insoluble food molecules into small soluble molecules that can be absorbed
It makes food hotter so that it dissolves faster
It turns all food molecules into starch, which the body can absorb
It removes water from food so the molecules become smaller
quiz.rationale: Starch, proteins and fats are large and insoluble. Enzymes break them into small soluble molecules such as sugars, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol, which can be absorbed.
quiz.placement: End of lesson: summary sentence on the annotated digestive-system model

lessons.title: Absorption, Assimilation, and Malnutrition: From Villi to Village Health

quiz.prompt: In Lesson 8, enzymes broke the starch in ugali into glucose. Why must starch be broken down into glucose before the nutrient can pass from the small intestine into the blood?
choices: Glucose is sweet, and sweet substances can pass through the wall more easily
Pressure from the muscles of the gut squeezes whole starch molecules through the wall
Glucose molecules are small and soluble, so they can cross the thin intestine wall, but starch molecules are too large
Starch is absorbed in the stomach, so digestion only matters for fats
quiz.rationale: Only small, soluble molecules can cross the thin wall of the intestine. Enzyme action turns large starch molecules into glucose, which is small enough to be absorbed.
quiz.placement: Predict: two-sentence prediction on how small molecules get from the intestine into the blood

quiz.prompt: Which feature of the ileum wall gives it a very large surface area for absorbing nutrients?
choices: One large pouch that holds food for a long time
Finger-like villi whose surface cells have tiny microvilli (brush border)
A thick, smooth wall with no folds, so food slides along it quickly
A thick layer of muscle that squeezes nutrients into the blood
quiz.rationale: Villi project into the lumen, and the epithelial cells covering them have microvilli. Together they greatly increase the surface area available for absorption.
quiz.placement: Observe: structured observation table on the ileum wall, villus and microvilli diagram

quiz.prompt: After fatty acids and glycerol cross the epithelial cells of a villus, where do they go next?
choices: Into the stomach, where they are stored
Into the blood capillaries, then along the hepatic portal vein to the liver
Into the central lacteal, then along the lymphatic system
Straight back into the lumen of the intestine
quiz.rationale: Fatty acids and glycerol recombine into tiny fat droplets that enter the lacteal and travel in the lymph. Glucose and amino acids are the ones that enter the capillaries.
quiz.placement: Observe: two routes (blood capillaries versus lacteal) for different nutrients

quiz.prompt: Glucose from a meal of ugali crosses the wall of the small intestine and enters a blood capillary. Later, a muscle cell uses some of that glucose in cellular respiration to release energy. Which statement describes these two events correctly?
choices: Entering the blood is assimilation, and use in the muscle cell is absorption
Both events are assimilation
Entering the blood is absorption, and use in the muscle cell is assimilation
Both events are absorption
quiz.rationale: Absorption is the movement of digested nutrients from the intestine into the blood or lymph. Assimilation is the use of those nutrients by body cells, for example in respiration.
quiz.placement: Explain Part A: absorption and assimilation, two-sentence distinction

quiz.prompt: Carrier proteins in the epithelial cell membrane pull glucose and amino acids into the cell using energy. Why is this active transport useful in the small intestine?
choices: It lets large food particles pass through the wall without being digested
It allows the body to absorb glucose and amino acids even when their concentration in the gut is low
It breaks starch and proteins into smaller molecules
It only works when there is more glucose in the gut than in the blood
quiz.rationale: Diffusion only works from high to low concentration. Active transport uses energy, so nutrients can be absorbed even when the gut concentration is low.
quiz.placement: Explain Part A: what moves glucose across the thin epithelial wall (diffusion and active transport)

quiz.prompt: Glucose and amino acids enter the blood capillaries of a villus. Which vessel carries them away, and where does it take them first?
choices: The lymphatic system, to the lungs
The lacteal, to the heart
The hepatic portal vein, to the liver
The hepatic portal vein, to the kidneys
quiz.rationale: Glucose and amino acids travel in the blood from the villus capillaries along the hepatic portal vein to the liver. The lacteal and lymph route is for fats.
quiz.placement: Explain Part A: blue arrow annotation, capillaries to the hepatic portal vein

quiz.prompt: A five-year-old child in Kilifi eats mainly ugali and cassava, with very little fish or beans. The child has a swollen belly, flaking skin and stunted growth, and is diagnosed with kwashiorkor. Which nutrient is lacking, and which locally available foods would help?
choices: Water; drinking more water would cure it
Iron; sukuma wiki and liver
Carbohydrate; more ugali and cassava
Protein; beans, ndengu, omena and eggs
quiz.rationale: The diet is high in carbohydrate but very low in protein. Without enough amino acids the body cannot build and repair tissues, so the child is stunted and swollen. Beans, ndengu, omena and eggs supply protein.
quiz.placement: Explain Part B: Case Study 1, kwashiorkor in coastal Kenya

quiz.prompt: A teenage girl in Nairobi often skips meals and rarely eats dark leafy vegetables or meat. A test shows her haemoglobin is below the level used to define anaemia, and she feels tired and looks pale. What is the best explanation?
choices: She has too much iron, which blocks oxygen in the blood
She lacks iron, so she makes too little haemoglobin and fewer red blood cells carry oxygen to her cells
She lacks protein, so her villi cannot form
Her stomach absorbs too much food, so her blood becomes thin
quiz.rationale: Iron is needed to make haemoglobin. With too little iron, less oxygen reaches the cells, causing tiredness and paleness. This is iron-deficiency anaemia.
quiz.placement: Explain Part B: Case Study 2, iron-deficiency anaemia in adolescent girls in Nairobi

lessons.title: Synthesis and Model Finalisation: From Aphid Stylets to Human Villi — One Purpose, Many Structures

quiz.prompt: On a maize farm in Kakamega, a mosquito can drink a person's blood but a grasshopper cannot. Which explanation is best?
choices: The mosquito has a piercing-sucking proboscis that reaches liquid blood, while the grasshopper has chewing mandibles made for solid plant tissue.
Both insects have the same mouthparts, but the mosquito is lighter and so can reach blood.
The grasshopper has no stomach, so it cannot digest any food.
The mosquito has sharp teeth like a human, so it can bite through skin.
quiz.rationale: Mouthpart structure decides what food an insect can reach. The mosquito's proboscis pierces skin and sucks liquid blood, while the grasshopper's mandibles chew solid leaves.
quiz.placement: Predict: writing a 3-sentence answer to the driving question and comparing it with the Lesson 1 initial model

quiz.prompt: At Lake Nakuru, a flamingo sweeps its bent beak sideways through the water. A fish eagle on a branch tears a fish apart with its hooked beak. What best explains why their beaks are so different?
choices: The flamingo's beak is hooked at the tip for catching fish, while the eagle's beak has lamellae for filtering water.
The flamingo's beak has lamellae that filter tiny food from water, while the eagle's hooked beak is adapted for tearing flesh.
Both birds eat the same food, so their beaks only look different.
Beak shape is random and has no link to the food an animal eats.
quiz.rationale: Each beak is a structural adaptation to diet and feeding strategy. Lamellae filter small food from water, and a hooked beak tears flesh.
quiz.placement: Gallery Walk: peer review of finalised cumulative models showing the flamingo and fish eagle feeding structures

quiz.prompt: Aphids cluster on maize stems. The leaves stay whole, but the plant wilts. Which statement best explains this?
choices: The aphids chew the stem with strong mandibles and swallow solid pieces.
The aphids use needle-like stylets to pierce the stem and suck out plant sap, so the plant loses fluid and nutrients without leaf tissue being chewed.
The aphids filter tiny particles from the air using lamellae.
The aphids drink blood from the plant's roots using a proboscis.
quiz.rationale: The aphid's stylet is a needle-like mouthpart that taps sap, so it takes liquid food without making ragged chewing holes like the grasshopper.
quiz.placement: Gallery Walk: checking that models show the aphid stylet linked to structure, function and nutrient type

quiz.prompt: What is the main role of villi in the human small intestine?
choices: They greatly increase the surface area so digested nutrients are absorbed into the bloodstream quickly.
They make stomach acid that kills germs in food.
They absorb water only from undigested waste.
They churn food to break it into smaller pieces by mechanical digestion.
quiz.rationale: Villi are finger-like folds that increase the surface area of the small intestine. This lets digested nutrients be absorbed into the blood efficiently.
quiz.placement: Part A: Final Explanation (CER+Evidence), connecting feeding structure to digestion and absorption (villus diagram from Lesson 9)

quiz.prompt: A learner eats githeri (maize and beans). Which statement correctly describes what happens to the protein in the beans?
choices: Protease enzymes digest the protein into amino acids, which villi absorb into the bloodstream for growth and cell repair.
The protein is absorbed in the mouth, so no enzymes are needed.
The protein is changed into glucose in the large intestine and used only for energy.
Teeth chew the protein into small pieces, and these whole pieces are absorbed directly into the blood.
quiz.rationale: Chemical digestion by protease enzymes breaks protein into amino acids, which are small enough to be absorbed through the villi into the blood. Chewing only breaks food into smaller pieces.
quiz.placement: Part A: Final Explanation (CER+Evidence), reasoning from food type to digestion to absorption to survival

quiz.prompt: A family in Nairobi has a small budget. Approximate prices are: githeri KES 30 per plate, sukuma wiki KES 10 per bunch, ugali KES 20 per plate, mandazi KES 5 per piece, nyama choma KES 150 per portion. They want a meal with protein and also iron and vitamins. Which choice is best?
choices: Nyama choma only, because the most expensive food must be the most nutritious overall.
Githeri with sukuma wiki, because together they give energy, plant protein, iron and vitamins at a low cost.
Mandazi only, because it is the cheapest and is a complete food.
Ugali with mandazi, because they give the most energy for the least money.
quiz.rationale: No single food is complete. Githeri gives energy and plant protein, and sukuma wiki is a cheap source of iron and vitamins, so the pair costs only KES 40 and is better value than the other options.
quiz.placement: Part B: Kenyan Food Cost-Nutrition Analysis (githeri, sukuma wiki, ugali, mandazi, nyama choma)

quiz.prompt: The class has described the aphid stylet, grasshopper mandibles, mosquito proboscis, flamingo lamellae, fish eagle beak and human teeth. Which unifying idea links all of them?
choices: Only animals with teeth can obtain nutrients from their food.
Each structure is adapted to the animal's diet and feeding strategy, helping it get the nutrients it needs to survive.
Feeding structures vary at random and are not linked to food type.
All animals have the same mouthparts, which only look different in size.
quiz.rationale: The unit's unifying principle is that structure enables nutrient acquisition. Different structures suit different diets, but all serve the same purpose of getting nutrients for survival, growth and energy.
quiz.placement: Driving Question Board closure: Key Inquiry Question 1 and the question 'What is the unifying principle across ALL of these?'
